rows.experiment_summary: This experiment established the search baseline by testing the simplest RNA-only configuration (single profile, PCA-2000 encoder, no image, no fusion), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.485 with a supporting F1 of 0.464. As the first completed experiment, this result serves as the performance floor for RNA-based classification and provides the reference point against which all subsequent design choices (richer RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) will be measured. It remains uncertain whether this accuracy is near the ceiling achievable with RNA data alone or whether substantially richer representations or additional modalities could produce meaningful gains.
rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about the performance landscape. The most fundamental unknown is the baseline performance of the simplest possible model. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal RNA-only configuration, using a simple linear PCA projection as the encoder. It establishes the performance floor for RNA-based classification and tells us how much predictive signal is present in the raw transcriptomic data without any learned or nonlinear representation. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Starting from the simplest configuration provides a clean reference point against which every subsequent design choice (better RNA encoders like scvi/scgpt, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be measured. If this baseline is already strong, it tells us the RNA signal is sufficient and we should focus on marginal gains; if it is weak, it motivates exploring richer encoders or additional modalities. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the starting point of the entire search and is the natural anchor for all future comparisons.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested the image-only modality (single profile, ResNet50 encoder, no fusion) to isolate whether image features carry useful signal for the task, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), substantially below the RNA-only baseline of 0.485 (F1 0.464). The result suggests that, under this simple pipeline, image features alone provide considerably less discriminative signal than RNA features, positioning RNA as the more promising anchor modality for subsequent experiments. It remains uncertain whether a different image encoder, alternative preprocessing, or multimodal fusion with RNA could recover meaningful signal from the image channel, so the image modality is not yet definitively ruled out.
rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only completed experiment (config_001, RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile) yields 0.485 accuracy, establishing a floor but leaving the most fundamental question unanswered: does the image modality carry useful signal for this task at all? Without knowing this, the search space splits into two very different strategies (RNA-focused vs. multimodal), and ~30 of the 51 configurations become irrelevant if image is uninformative. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) isolates the modality question with the simplest possible image pipeline, directly comparable in structural complexity to config_001. It tells us whether image features alone can approach, match, or exceed the RNA-only baseline, which determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and which modality should be the anchor. 3) Why best use of budget: With only one data point, the highest-value experiment is the one that most sharply reduces uncertainty about a top-level design axis. The modality question is more fundamental than encoder choice or profile aggregation—its answer will prune or prioritize large swaths of the remaining search space, making every subsequent experiment more targeted. Testing a richer RNA encoder (e.g., scvi) or multiprofile aggregation would be informative but less decisive, since those improvements are only relevant within the RNA branch and do not resolve whether the image channel should be included at all.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment isolated the RNA encoder effect by replacing PCA-2000 with scvi_n200 while holding all other settings (RNA-only, single profile, no fusion) constant relative to the llm_summary_001 baseline, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1 0.498) versus 0.485 (F1 0.464) for PCA-2000. Because only the encoder changed, this single-variable comparison indicates that a learned non-linear representation captures structure that PCA-2000 misses, but the ~3.5-point gain is moderate rather than transformative, suggesting the RNA representation is a contributing but not dominant bottleneck. It remains uncertain whether further encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt) would yield larger gains, whether the improvement plateaus within the RNA-only regime, or whether multiprofile aggregation and multimodal fusion (with the image modality at 0.208 accuracy in llm_summary_002) could unlock substantially higher performance.
rows.selection_reason: With only two completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether the PCA-2000 encoder is near the RNA ceiling or whether a learned representation can substantially improve RNA-based classification. Config_004 (scvi_n200, single profile, RNA-only) changes exactly one factor from the config_001 baseline—the RNA encoder—while holding profile setting, modality, and fusion constant. This cleanly isolates the encoder effect. If scvi_n200 meaningfully outperforms PCA-2000 (0.485), it indicates the representation is a bottleneck and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and richer multimodal builds. If it performs similarly, it suggests PCA already captures most useful linear structure, redirecting effort toward multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion. Given the sparse evidence, this single-variable comparison is the highest-information-per-experiment choice before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested the effect of multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) by switching from single-profile to multiprofile while holding the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and all other settings constant relative to llm_summary_003, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.650 (F1 0.628) versus 0.520 (F1 0.498) for the single-profile configuration. Because only the profile/aggregation design changed, this clean single-variable comparison indicates that aggregating multiple profiles per cell with a simple average pool captures substantially more discriminative signal than a single profile—a ~13-point gain far exceeding the ~3.5-point encoder improvement observed earlier. It remains uncertain whether a more sophisticated aggregation strategy (e.g., transformer-based) could push accuracy further, whether the multiprofile gain generalizes to other RNA encoders, or whether combining multiprofile aggregation with the image modality or fusion could yield additional improvements.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: RNA-only single-profile with scvi_n200 achieves 0.520 accuracy (vs 0.485 for PCA-2000), confirming RNA as the dominant modality and scvi_n200 as the current best encoder. Image-only is weak (0.208). The multiprofile axis is completely unexplored—zero experiments have tested whether aggregating multiple profiles per cell adds signal. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the effect of the multiprofile+aggregation design decision while holding the encoder at the currently best performer (scvi_n200). avgpool is the simplest aggregation, making this a clean first test of whether multiprofile helps at all. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it opens a completely new axis with no prior information, which is more informative than a third encoder comparison (scgpt) where the PCA→scvi gain was already modest (~3.5 pts), suggesting we may be near the single-profile RNA ceiling; (2) if multiprofile+avgpool yields a meaningful gain, it justifies testing transformer aggregation (config_006) and multiprofile variants of other encoders; if it does not help, we can deprioritize the entire multiprofile branch and save budget; (3) it uses the best-known encoder, so any gain or loss is attributable to the profile/aggregation decision rather than confounded by a weaker representation.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested transformer-based aggregation in the multiprofile RNA-only setting (scvi_n200 encoder) as a single-variable comparison against the avgpool configuration (llm_summary_004), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.653 (F1 0.628) versus 0.650 (F1 0.628) for avgpool. The ~0.3-point accuracy gain and near-identical F1 suggest that, under this configuration, transformer aggregation captures at most a marginal improvement over simple average pooling, indicating that the aggregation strategy is unlikely to be a dominant remaining bottleneck within the multiprofile regime. It remains uncertain whether this small difference is statistically meaningful, whether other aggregation architectures or transformer hyperparameter tuning could yield larger gains, or whether further improvements are more likely to come from encoder exploration (e.g., scgpt) or multimodal fusion.
rows.selection_reason: The strongest result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy, showing that multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever (~13-point gain over single profile). The key remaining uncertainty within this promising regime is whether the aggregation strategy itself can be improved: does a transformer-based aggregation capture inter-profile relationships that a simple average pool misses? config_006 is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (only aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer), directly isolating the aggregation effect. This is the best use of the next experiment because: (1) it exploits the strongest evidence by testing a logical extension of the best configuration, (2) it reduces uncertainty about a design choice that will propagate into all future multimodal experiments, and (3) the answer—whether transformer helps, hurts, or is neutral—will determine whether to invest further in aggregation complexity or pivot to encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal fusion. No other single experiment provides as much information per trial at this stage.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested scgpt as the RNA encoder in the multiprofile + avgpool RNA-only setting as a clean single-variable comparison against scvi_n200 (llm_summary_004), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.530 (F1 0.515) versus 0.650 (F1 0.628) for scvi_n200. The ~12-point accuracy drop indicates that, under multiprofile aggregation, scgpt does not outperform scvi_n200 and in fact performs substantially worse, confirming scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA backbone for this task in the multiprofile regime. It remains uncertain whether scgpt's underperformance reflects a training or hyperparameter issue rather than a fundamental representational limitation, whether it could perform differently under alternative aggregation strategies or in multimodal fusion, and whether the multiprofile gain is specific to scvi_n200's learned structure.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: The multiprofile + avgpool + scvi_n200 configuration (config_005) achieved 0.650 accuracy, representing the largest gain so far (~13 pts over single-profile). The encoder comparison (scvi_n200 vs PCA-2000) showed a moderate ~3.5 pt gain, and aggregation strategy (transformer vs avgpool) showed negligible difference. Uncertainty: It remains unknown whether scgpt, a more expressive learned RNA encoder, provides a meaningful improvement over scvi_n200 in the multiprofile regime where the biggest gains are realized. Question: config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, isolating the encoder effect (scvi_n200 → scgpt) while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Resolving the encoder question before investing in multimodal fusion is critical—multimodal configurations introduce multiple new variables (image encoder, fusion strategy), and committing to a suboptimal RNA encoder would confound those comparisons. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, it redefines the best RNA backbone for all downstream fusion experiments; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 is sufficient and can pivot to testing whether the weak image modality (0.208 alone) adds complementary signal via fusion. This single experiment reduces the most important remaining uncertainty in the RNA representation dimension at minimal cost.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested the simplest multimodal extension of the best RNA-only configuration by adding ResNet50 image features via concat fusion to the scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool pipeline, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.632 (F1 0.607) versus 0.650 (F1 0.628) for the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_004). Because only the image channel and concat fusion were introduced relative to that baseline, this single-variable comparison indicates that, under this specific configuration, the ResNet50 image features do not provide complementary discriminative signal and instead slightly degrade performance by approximately 1.9 accuracy points. It remains uncertain whether alternative fusion strategies (e.g., gated or attention-based), different image encoders, or adjusted image preprocessing could recover meaningful multimodal gains, or whether the RNA-only multiprofile pipeline is already near the achievable ceiling for this task.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool at ~0.650 accuracy (config_005/006). The most important remaining uncertainty is whether adding the image modality via fusion can improve upon this strong RNA-only baseline. Although image-only performance is weak (0.208 with ResNet50), that does not preclude complementary signal in a fused setting. Config_030 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50, concat) is the simplest multimodal extension of the best RNA-only configuration, changing only the addition of the image channel with the most straightforward fusion (concat). A positive result would open a new optimization axis (fusion strategy, image encoder); a negative or neutral result would confirm that the RNA-only multiprofile pipeline is near the achievable ceiling and redirect effort toward other levers. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it directly tests the single largest unexplored design dimension (modality combination) while holding all other variables at their empirically best settings.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested weighted fusion as the sole change relative to concat fusion (llm_summary_007), keeping the scvi_n200/multiprofile/avgpool backbone and ResNet50 image encoder constant, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.678 (F1 0.646) versus 0.632 (F1 0.607) for concat fusion. Because only the fusion strategy changed, this clean single-variable comparison indicates that weighted fusion recovers and exceeds the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (0.650, llm_summary_004) by ~2.8 accuracy points, suggesting that ResNet50 image features do carry complementary discriminative signal but require learned gating to be effectively integrated rather than naively concatenated. It remains uncertain whether more sophisticated fusion strategies (e.g., attention-based), a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), or further tuning of the weighted fusion could yield additional gains, or whether the current configuration is near the achievable multimodal ceiling for this task.
rows.selection_reason: Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 accuracy. Adding ResNet50 image features via concat fusion (config_030) slightly degrades performance to 0.632, suggesting the image channel introduces noise or that concat is too aggressive a combination strategy. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the ~2-point degradation is an artifact of the naive concat fusion (which equally weights all features) or a fundamental lack of complementary signal in ResNet50 image features. This experiment (config_031) tests weighted fusion as the sole change relative to config_030, isolating the fusion strategy effect while keeping the proven scvi_n200/multiprofile/avgpool backbone and ResNet50 encoder constant. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds 0.650, it indicates the image carries complementary signal that requires learned gating; if it also fails to beat the RNA-only baseline, it strongly suggests ResNet50 features are uninformative for this task regardless of fusion, directing future budget toward either a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or confirming RNA-only as the optimal architecture. This is the cleanest, most interpretable single-variable follow-up and the highest-information next step under a limited budget.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested the effect of upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) constant relative to llm_summary_008, yielding a validation accuracy of 0.706 (F1 0.667) versus 0.678 (F1 0.646) for ResNet50. Because only the image encoder changed, this clean single-variable comparison indicates that the image channel's contribution was partially encoder-limited: the stronger ViT-L backbone unlocks approximately 2.9 additional accuracy points of complementary signal, bringing the total multimodal gain over the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (0.650, llm_summary_004) to roughly 5.6 points. It remains uncertain whether further encoder scaling, alternative fusion strategies, or additional tuning could extract more signal from the image modality, or whether the current configuration is approaching the achievable ceiling for this task.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_031: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, ResNet50) achieves 0.678 accuracy, but the image channel's contribution is uncertain because ResNet50 was very weak in isolation (0.208 accuracy image-only). The key question is whether the image modality's ~2.8-point gain over RNA-only is encoder-limited (i.e., a stronger encoder like ViT-L could unlock more complementary signal) or fundamentally limited by the image data's discriminative content. Config_037 changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) constant, providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_031. This is the highest-information next experiment: if ViT-L substantially improves accuracy, it confirms the image channel has untapped potential and justifies further multimodal investment; if it does not, it indicates the image contribution is near its ceiling and the current configuration is close to optimal. This is preferred over testing transformer aggregation (config_033), which is low-value given the near-identical RNA-only results (0.653 vs 0.650), and over changing multiple variables simultaneously.

rows.experiment_summary: This experiment tested transformer aggregation as a clean single-variable change from the prior best configuration (llm_summary_009: avgpool, ViT-L, weighted fusion), yielding a validation accuracy of 0.725 (F1 0.685) versus 0.706 (F1 0.667) for avgpool—a ~1.9-point accuracy gain. This gain is substantially larger than the ~0.3-point difference observed between transformer and avgpool in the RNA-only multiprofile regime (llm_summary_005 vs llm_summary_004), suggesting that in the multimodal setting the more expressive aggregation captures profile-level structure that better complements the ViT-L image signal under weighted fusion. It remains uncertain whether further aggregation tuning, alternative fusion strategies, or encoder scaling could yield additional gains, or whether the current configuration is approaching the achievable ceiling for this task.
rows.selection_reason: The current best configuration (config_037: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 accuracy. In the RNA-only regime, transformer aggregation gave only a negligible 0.3-point gain over avgpool (config_006 vs config_005), suggesting aggregation is not a major bottleneck. However, that comparison was made without an image modality; in the multimodal setting, the aggregation step operates on RNA profiles before fusion with image features, and a more expressive aggregation could theoretically capture profile-level structure that better complements the image signal. Config_039 is a clean single-variable change from the current best (avgpool → transformer), isolating the aggregation effect in the multimodal ViT-L + weighted fusion context. If it yields a meaningful gain, it identifies a new best and a productive direction; if it confirms the RNA-only finding of negligible difference, it definitively rules out aggregation as a remaining lever, allowing us to redirect remaining budget toward other design axes (e.g., fusion refinement or encoder scaling) with confidence. Under the limited budget, this is the highest-information single-variable test available from the current frontier.
